```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "~/arabidopsis_project")
```

## 1. What this does

RIS-PCR was the best-performing method so far (MSPE 107.93 vs RIS-RP's 170.43, same
8,718 screened SNPs, same everything else -- only the projection differs: real
principal components instead of a random matrix). This document:

1. Reproduces that exact screened, standardized training matrix
2. Runs a full PCA study on it -- variance explained per PC, cumulative variance,
   and a PC1-vs-PC2 view colored by flowering time
3. Refits the actual winning model and writes it out explicitly as
   $y = a_0 + a_1 \text{PC}_1 + a_2 \text{PC}_2 + \dots + a_{100}\text{PC}_{100}$,
   with the real fitted coefficients

```{r blas-fix}
if (!requireNamespace("RhpcBLASctl", quietly = TRUE)) {
  stop("Run in terminal first: micromamba install -c conda-forge r-rhpcblasctl")
}
RhpcBLASctl::blas_set_num_threads(1)
N_CORES <- 3

mem_check <- function(label) {
  g <- gc(full = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("[memory] %s: %.0f MB in use\n", label, sum(g[, 2])))
}
```

## 2. Reproduce the screened, standardized data (same seeds as before)

```{r reproduce-screening}
library(bigsnpr); library(bigstatsr)

obj.bigSNP <- snp_attach("arabidopsis_1135_matched.rds")
G <- obj.bigSNP$genotypes; fam <- obj.bigSNP$fam
pheno <- read.csv("flowering_time.csv")
y_all <- pheno$FT10[match(as.character(fam$sample.ID), as.character(pheno$accession_id))]
n <- nrow(G); p <- ncol(G)

G2 <- snp_fastImputeSimple(G, method = "mean2", ncores = N_CORES)

set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(n), size = round(0.8 * n))
test_idx  <- setdiff(seq_len(n), train_idx)
y_train <- y_all[train_idx]; y_test <- y_all[test_idx]
y_mean  <- mean(y_train);    y_train_c <- y_train - y_mean

gwas <- big_univLinReg(G2, y.train = y_all, ncores = N_CORES)
t_stat <- gwas$estim / gwas$std.err
r <- sign(t_stat) * sqrt(t_stat^2 / (t_stat^2 + (n - 2))); r[is.na(r)] <- 0
delta <- max(0, (1 + log(p / n)) / 2)
q <- abs(r)^delta; q <- q / max(q)
set.seed(1)
included_rp <- which(rbinom(p, 1, q) == 1)
cat("Screened SNPs:", length(included_rp), "(should match earlier run: 8718)\n")

X_s <- G2[, included_rp]
col_mean <- colMeans(X_s[train_idx, ]); col_sd <- apply(X_s[train_idx, ], 2, sd); col_sd[col_sd == 0] <- 1
X_train_s <- scale(X_s[train_idx, ], center = col_mean, scale = col_sd)
X_test_s  <- scale(X_s[test_idx, ],  center = col_mean, scale = col_sd)
rm(X_s, G); mem_check("after reproducing screened matrix")
```

## 3. Full PCA on the screened, standardized training matrix

Capped at the top 300 components rather than the full 801 possible -- in genomic data
this dense with linkage disequilibrium, variance beyond a few hundred components is
essentially noise, and 300 is already 3x the 100 the model actually uses, enough to
see the full decay shape without an unnecessarily heavy computation.

```{r full-pca}
pca_full <- prcomp(X_train_s, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE, rank. = 300)
mem_check("after full PCA")

var_explained <- (pca_full$sdev^2) / sum(pca_full$sdev^2) * 100
cum_var <- cumsum(var_explained)

cat("Variance explained by first 10 PCs (%):\n")
print(round(var_explained[1:10], 2))

cat("\nPCs needed to reach:\n")
cat("  50% variance:", which(cum_var >= 50)[1], "\n")
cat("  80% variance:", which(cum_var >= 80)[1], "\n")
cat("  90% variance:", which(cum_var >= 90)[1], "\n")
cat("  Variance explained by first 100 PCs (used in the model):", round(cum_var[100], 2), "%\n")
```

## 4. Plot: scree plot (variance explained per PC)

```{r scree-plot}
plot(1:100, var_explained[1:100], type = "b", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     xlab = "Principal Component", ylab = "Variance Explained (%)",
     main = "Scree Plot -- First 100 PCs")
abline(v = 100, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

## 5. Plot: cumulative variance explained

```{r cumulative-variance}
# note: prcomp's rank. only truncates $rotation/$x, not $sdev -- cum_var is the
# FULL spectrum (length ~801 here), so we plot against its actual length rather
# than assuming it matches the rank. cap used for the loadings
plot(seq_along(cum_var), cum_var, type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Number of Principal Components", ylab = "Cumulative Variance Explained (%)",
     main = sprintf("Cumulative Variance Explained -- All %d Components", length(cum_var)))
abline(h = c(50, 80, 90), col = "gray50", lty = 3)
abline(v = 100, col = "red", lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", legend = c("50/80/90% reference", "100 PCs (used in model)"),
       col = c("gray50", "red"), lty = c(3, 2), bty = "n")
```

## 6. Plot: PC1 vs PC2, colored by flowering time

If PC1/PC2 mostly track geography (population structure) rather than flowering time,
you'll see color scattered fairly evenly across the point cloud rather than forming a
clean gradient along one axis.

```{r pc1-pc2-scatter}
scores <- pca_full$x[, 1:2]
col_ramp <- colorRampPalette(c("blue", "yellow", "red"))(100)
y_bin <- cut(y_train, breaks = 100, labels = FALSE)

plot(scores[, 1], scores[, 2], col = col_ramp[y_bin], pch = 19, cex = 0.8,
     xlab = "PC1", ylab = "PC2", main = "PC1 vs PC2, colored by FT10 (blue=low, red=high)")
```

## 7. Refit the winning model (RIS-PCR) using the first 100 PCs

```{r refit-model}
m_n <- 100
Z_train <- X_train_s %*% pca_full$rotation[, 1:m_n]
Z_test  <- X_test_s  %*% pca_full$rotation[, 1:m_n]

a_sigma <- 0.01; b_sigma <- 0.01
A <- diag(m_n) + t(Z_train) %*% Z_train
mu_t <- solve(A) %*% t(Z_train) %*% y_train_c

pred_test <- (Z_test %*% mu_t) + y_mean
mspe <- mean((y_test - pred_test)^2)
cat("RIS-PCR Test MSPE (sanity check, should match 107.93):", mspe, "\n")
```

## 8. Plot: fitted coefficient for each of the 100 PCs used

```{r coef-plot}
coefs <- as.numeric(mu_t)
barplot(coefs, names.arg = 1:m_n, las = 2, cex.names = 0.5,
        xlab = "Principal Component", ylab = "Coefficient (a_k)",
        main = "Fitted Coefficients, y = a0 + sum(a_k * PC_k)", col = "steelblue", border = NA)
abline(h = 0, col = "gray30")
```

## 9. The final model, written out explicitly

```{r final-model}
a0 <- y_mean
ranked <- order(abs(coefs), decreasing = TRUE)

cat("Final fitted model:\n")
cat(sprintf("y = %.3f", a0))
for (k in ranked[1:10]) {
  sign_str <- if (coefs[k] >= 0) " + " else " - "
  cat(sprintf("%s%.4f * PC%d", sign_str, abs(coefs[k]), k))
}
cat(" + ... (90 more PC terms)\n\n")

cat("Top 10 PCs by contribution (|coefficient|):\n")
top10 <- data.frame(PC = ranked[1:10], coefficient = round(coefs[ranked[1:10]], 4),
                     variance_explained_pct = round(var_explained[ranked[1:10]], 2))
print(top10)

cat("\nFull model uses all 100 PCs; a0 =", round(a0, 3),
    "(this is just mean(y_train) -- the model predicts deviations from it)\n")

saveRDS(list(a0 = a0, coefs = coefs, rotation = pca_full$rotation[, 1:m_n],
             col_mean = col_mean, col_sd = col_sd, included_rp = included_rp),
        "final_pca_model.rds")
cat("Saved final_pca_model.rds\n")
```

## 10. Honest notes

- $a_0$ is just $\bar{y}_{train}$ -- the model's baseline is the mean, and every PC
  term is a *deviation* from it.
- A PC with a large coefficient but low variance-explained is a PC that captures a
  small share of total genetic variation but is disproportionately predictive of
  flowering time -- worth flagging as a candidate for the "which underlying SNPs load
  heavily on this PC" follow-up question.
- These are principal components of the **screened SNP matrix**, not raw SNPs --
  translating a PC back into "which genes/positions matter" requires looking at
  `pca_full$rotation[, k]`, the loading of each of the 8,718 screened SNPs on PC k.

## 11. Exploiting orthogonality: does adding more PCs improve held-out MSPE?

Because PCs from one decomposition are mutually orthogonal, and the NIG posterior
here uses an isotropic (diagonal) prior, every PC's coefficient is *exactly* the
same whether fit alone, in a batch, or jointly with all the others:
$\mu_{t,j} = Z_j'y_c / (1+Z_j'Z_j)$, independent of what else is in the model. So
instead of refitting from scratch for each PC count, we compute every PC's
coefficient once and just extend the slice.

**This does not generalize to RIS-RP or GSIS** -- a random projection matrix's
output columns are not orthogonal, so this shortcut is specific to PCA.

```{r pc-count-sweep}
Z_full_train <- X_train_s %*% pca_full$rotation
d_j   <- colSums(Z_full_train^2)
mu_all <- colSums(Z_full_train * y_train_c) / (1 + d_j)

Z_full_test <- X_test_s %*% pca_full$rotation

pc_counts <- c(10, 25, 50, 100, 150, 200, 246, 300)
mspe_by_count <- sapply(pc_counts, function(k) {
  pred <- (Z_full_test[, 1:k, drop = FALSE] %*% mu_all[1:k]) + y_mean
  mean((y_test - pred)^2)
})

results_sweep <- data.frame(n_PCs = pc_counts,
                             cum_variance_pct = round(cum_var[pc_counts], 1),
                             Test_MSPE = round(mspe_by_count, 2))
print(results_sweep)

plot(pc_counts, mspe_by_count, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Number of PCs used", ylab = "Test MSPE",
     main = "Test MSPE vs Number of PCs (via orthogonality shortcut)")
abline(h = 107.93, col = "blue", lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = "m_n=100 result (107.93)", col = "blue", lty = 2, bty = "n")
```

**Caveat, restated precisely:** the MSPE numbers above are exact point predictions,
unaffected by the uncertainty-decomposition issue -- that issue only affects formal
credible intervals, not this curve.

## 12. Regression lines for the top PCs, one panel, using the model's own coefficients

Each subplot's line is $y = a_0 + a_k \cdot \text{PC}_k$ using the *actual* fitted
coefficient from the model (section 9/11) -- not a separately re-estimated OLS line.
Because of the orthogonality property, these are exactly the marginal slices of the
real additive model, term by term. Ranked by contribution (`|coefficient|`), not by
variance-explained order -- change `top_n` to 10 for a smaller grid.

```{r top-pc-panel, fig.width=14, fig.height=10}
top_n <- 20   # set to 10 for a 2x5 grid instead
top_pcs <- ranked[1:top_n]
n_row <- ceiling(top_n / 5)

par(mfrow = c(n_row, 5), mar = c(3, 3, 2.5, 1), mgp = c(2, 0.7, 0))
for (k in top_pcs) {
  x <- pca_full$x[, k]   # this PC's training scores
  plot(x, y_train, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "gray40",
       xlab = paste0("PC", k), ylab = "FT10",
       main = sprintf("PC%d  a=%.2f  var=%.1f%%", k, coefs[k], var_explained[k]),
       cex.main = 0.85)
  abline(a = y_mean, b = coefs[k], col = "red", lwd = 2)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Reading this panel:** a PC with a visibly steep red line and a tight scatter
around it is doing real predictive work. A PC with a high `var=` (explains a lot of
genetic variation) but a flat line contributes little to flowering time despite
being a major axis of genetic variation -- likely population structure rather than
signal. A PC with a low `var=` but a steep line is the more interesting case: a
minor share of total genetic variation that happens to matter disproportionately for
the phenotype.
